title: Singapore's Monetary Policy: A Case Study in Rate Lag
abstract: Singapore's monetary policy is a masterclass in watching the world change while your dial stays stuck.
body:
## The Great Singapore Rate Stare-Down

I have a confession: I love Singapore. I love the food, the efficiency, the way the MRT makes other cities look like they're running on diesel and spite. But I cannot love Singapore's monetary policy. It is, and I say this with affection, a relic. The Monetary Authority of Singapore runs a basket-band regime, tweaking the slope and width of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted path. It's clever. It's also slow. And in a world where the Bank of Japan can pivot on a dime and TSMC's order book can flip a currency's fortunes in a quarter, slow is a liability.

Let me be clear: I'm not against managed exchange rates. I'm against managed exchange rates that pretend the world hasn't changed since 1981. The MAS meets twice a year, maybe three times if the sky is falling. By the time it adjusts the slope, the shock has already washed through the economy. You want to talk about lag? This is lag as a lifestyle.

## The Bank of Japan Moves, Singapore Watches

Consider the Bank of Japan. For years, it was the world's most reliable source of free money. Then it blinked. A rate hike here, a yield curve tweak there, and suddenly the yen carry trade unwound like a cheap sweater. Global markets shuddered. Singapore? The MAS probably scheduled a meeting to discuss scheduling a meeting. That's not a central bank; that's a committee with a calendar.

I'm being unfair. The MAS doesn't set interest rates; it manages the exchange rate. Fine. But the exchange rate is a price, and prices move faster than committees. When the BoJ shifts, the Singapore dollar's effective rate should shift too. Instead, we get a polite adjustment every six months. It's like watching a chess grandmaster play speed chess with a sundial.

The result is predictable: Singapore imports the world's monetary policy with a delay. When the Fed hikes, Singapore feels it later. When the BoJ cuts, Singapore feels it later. Later is fine if you're a fine wine. It's less fine if you're an economy that lives and dies by trade.

## TSMC Sneezes, Singapore Catches a Cold

Here's another thing. Singapore's economy is not a closed loop. It's a node in a global supply chain that runs through Taiwan, South Korea, and increasingly Vietnam. TSMC is the world's most important company you've never bought a product from. When TSMC has a bad quarter, the ripple hits Singapore's electronics exports. When TSMC has a good quarter, Singapore's factories hum.

But the MAS doesn't react to TSMC. It reacts to a basket of currencies. That basket includes the currencies of countries that also react to TSMC. So you get a second-order effect: TSMC moves, those currencies move, the basket moves, and six months later the MAS adjusts the slope. By then, the cycle has turned. It's monetary policy as archaeology.

I'm not saying the MAS should abandon the basket. I'm saying it should abandon the calendar. The world doesn't wait for your semi-annual meeting. The Bank of Japan doesn't wait. TSMC doesn't wait. Why should Singapore?

## The Case for Chaos

Here's a radical idea: what if the MAS met more often? What if it adjusted the slope in real time, or at least quarterly? What if it stopped pretending that a six-month lag is a feature and not a bug?

I know the counterargument. Singapore is small, open, and vulnerable. A volatile exchange rate would scare off foreign investment. You need stability. You need predictability. You need a central bank that doesn't jerk the wheel every time a foreign central bank sneezes.

But stability isn't the same as rigidity. You can have a predictable framework with more frequent adjustments. You can have a basket-band system that responds to shocks without waiting for the next scheduled meeting. You can have a central bank that watches the Bank of Japan and TSMC and the Fed and reacts in weeks, not months.

The MAS won't do this. It's too proud of its regime. It's too invested in the idea that Singapore is different, that its monetary policy is a marvel of technocratic engineering. And maybe it was, in 1981. But in 2026, it's a case study in rate lag. The world has moved on. The MAS is still reading the minutes from the last meeting.

## What I'd Do Instead

If I ran the MAS, and thank God I don't, I'd start by admitting that the semi-annual cycle is arbitrary. I'd move to quarterly adjustments, with emergency meetings when the BoJ or the Fed does something stupid. I'd publish a real-time index of the Singapore dollar's effective rate, so everyone can see the lag. I'd stop pretending that a basket of currencies is a proxy for the global economy when the global economy is increasingly a proxy for TSMC.

I'd also stop calling it a "policy band." It's a policy straitjacket. The band is so wide that it's meaningless, and the slope is so gradual that it's invisible. You could replace the MAS with a thermostat and get the same result, except the thermostat would react faster.

Look, I get it. Singapore is a small country with a big financial center. It needs credibility. It needs stability. But credibility doesn't come from being slow. It comes from being right. And right now, the MAS is slow and wrong. It's fighting the last war, the one where exchange rates were the only tool that mattered. The new war is about speed. The Bank of Japan gets it. TSMC gets it. The MAS? Not so much.

So here's my advice to the MAS: set an alarm. Meet more often. Watch the world in real time. And for the love of all that is holy, stop pretending that a six-month lag is a strategy. It's not. It's a nap. And while you're napping, the rest of us are trading.
